rationale: This reruns the round-1 idea with the crash fixed. Round 1 failed only because it wrote into a read-only `.values` view; this version builds the matrix in a writable numpy array. The idea itself is unchanged. Each study shifts how abundant each genus looks, so the forest can partly learn batch effects. Z-scoring the log relative abundance of each genus within its study removes that shift without using labels. A one-hot study indicator keeps each study's different case/control ratio available to the model.

Lower alpha diversity is one of the most reproducible stool signatures of IBD (dysbiosis). The forest only sees individual genera, so it can't easily rebuild a whole-community diversity summary from them. This change adds OTU- and genus-level Shannon entropy, genus-level inverse Simpson, and a depth-robust richness measure (OTUs above 1e-4 relative abundance). Each is z-scored within its study, the same way the genus features are, so differences in sequencing depth and protocol between studies cancel out.

Different 16S regions and pipelines resolve OTUs to genus at very different rates. So many reads, including key IBD signals like Enterobacteriaceae, Lachnospiraceae and Ruminococcaceae, end up in the single global `g__` bucket, where they mix across families and the signal is lost. This change adds log relative abundance at family level, keyed by the full lineage down to family and z-scored within each study. That keeps the unclassified-genus reads inside their family, and family level is more consistent across studies than genus level.

Gevers et al. (2014, the RISK cohort in this pool) describe IBD dysbiosis as a combined shift: taxa that rise in IBD (Enterobacteriaceae, Pasteurellaceae, Fusobacteriaceae, Neisseriaceae, Veillonellaceae, Gemellaceae) go up while the commensal anaerobes (Bacteroidales, Clostridiales apart from Veillonellaceae, Erysipelotrichaceae, Bifidobacteriaceae) go down. A random forest splitting on single genera cannot easily form that pooled log-ratio, so this change adds their microbial dysbiosis index as a known-marker feature. It is computed from family and order names, which are more consistent across studies than genus names, and z-scored within each study like the other features.

IBD dysbiosis shows up as many small shifts in the same direction across lots of genera, and individual RF splits approximate that poorly. I'm adding an L2 logistic regression on the same within-study z-scored features and averaging its probabilities with the RF's. Its strength C is picked by grouped inner CV on the training fold, so the linear model can capture that additive signal while the forest keeps the nonlinear one.

After pooling, the genus table probably contains many rare genera, and many of them may show up in only one study because of its sequencing region or classifier. Within that study they are noise, and in the other studies z-scoring makes them constant zero. With max_features=sqrt they dilute each RF split's candidate set and push the trees toward study-specific splits. This change keeps only genera that are reasonably prevalent (detected in ≥10% of samples) in at least two studies. That should focus the forest on taxa that are comparable across studies and likely to transfer. The filter is label-free and computed in featurize.

I'm replacing the within-study z-score with a within-study percentile rank (average ranks for ties, scaled to (0,1)). A z-score only shifts and rescales each study's values. That can't line up genus distributions that are full of zeros and skewed in different ways, or that have different detection floors because each study sequenced to a different depth. Ranking within each study gives every study the same distribution for each genus, so a forest split threshold means "the same relative position within its own cohort" in every study. That should cut down the leftover batch-specific splits.

Case/control ratios differ a lot between studies, and pooled AUROC rewards using each study's prior. In the current forest, though, that prior lives only in a few study one-hot columns that `max_features=sqrt` rarely offers to a split, so the RF uses it unevenly and badly calibrated. This change trains the RF only on the within-study z-scored microbiome features (the within-study evidence). It then gets out-of-fold RF scores from grouped inner CV and fits a small logistic model on [logit(RF score), study one-hots]. That model learns how much weight the RF evidence deserves and adds each study's prior as an explicit intercept, so both are combined properly.

After within-study z-scoring, zero counts land on a different value in each study, because each study has its own detection floor. The RF's exhaustive threshold search can lock onto those exact study-specific boundaries and learn batch structure instead of disease signal. This change swaps the RF for ExtraTrees (1000 trees, min_samples_leaf=2), which picks split thresholds at random; that should make it less likely to fit these artefacts, and it averages many more decorrelated trees, giving smoother, better-ranked probabilities for pooled AUROC.

I'm replacing the genus log relative abundance (fixed 1e-5 pseudocount) with a centred log-ratio (CLR) transform computed on genus counts with a 0.5 pseudocount, then z-scoring within study as before. Relative abundances are compositional: an IBD bloom of Enterobacteriaceae makes every commensal look smaller. CLR removes that closure effect. The count-based pseudocount also means a zero in a deeply sequenced sample gets a lower value than a zero in a shallow one, so it reflects depth instead of using one floor for every sample.

This round adds a CatBoost model next to the ExtraTrees forest and averages their probabilities. CatBoost builds shallow trees one after another, each correcting the last. Its ordered boosting is designed to overfit less on small, noisy samples. I expect it to pick up interactions the bagged trees miss, such as study one-hot × taxon effects and diversity × bloom-taxon combinations. ExtraTrees' randomized averaging should keep the ensemble robust.

IBD stool samples spread away from the healthy community state, so I'm adding a "dysbiosis score" in the style of Gevers 2014 and Halfvarson 2017. For each sample it measures the median Bray-Curtis distance, and the mean of the 5 nearest distances, to training-fold controls from the same study. The score is computed in `fit_predict` and leaves out the sample's own subject. It is then z-scored within study, which gives the trees a single community-level beta-diversity signal that holds up against batch effects and that they can't build from single-genus splits.

Studies were sequenced to very different depths, so the smallest abundance a study can detect (about 1/reads) ranges from roughly 1e-5 to 1e-3. Below that limit, a fixed 1e-5 pseudocount lets deep studies show tiny but real abundances and zeros, while shallow studies can only show zeros. In the pooled data that pattern tracks the study, not the disease. This change applies one shared detection limit to every sample (the 90th percentile of 1/depth, clipped to [1e-5, 1e-3]), much like rarefying to a common depth: genus abundances below the limit are set to the limit before the log and the within-study z-score. Zeros and near-detection values then mean the same thing in every study.

Round 14's common detection limit only touched the genus features. The diversity metrics still count OTUs down to 1e-4 and Shannon still uses every non-zero OTU, so they still depend on study-specific sequencing depth, which is the batch effect. This change censors OTU and genus abundances below the same shared limit (sets them to zero and renormalizes) before computing Shannon, inverse Simpson and richness. That is a cheap stand-in for rarefaction, so the diversity loss that marks IBD is measured at the same resolution in every study.

Rounds 3 and 15 showed that diversity measured at a resolution shared by all studies is a strong, transferable IBD signal. But every current metric counts OTUs and genera as equal and unrelated, and IBD dysbiosis tends to remove whole clades (Clostridiales and Bacteroidales families). This change adds a taxonomy-aware, Faith-PD-like measure: the number of distinct lineage nodes, across all ranks, that hold OTUs above the shared detection limit, where each level of the RDP tree counts as one unit of branch length. It also adds family-level richness and Shannon entropy. All are computed on the same floor-censored profiles and z-scored within study.
